title: Instructions and the imperative
objectives: I can build the affirmative and negative command form for 'você' and 'vocês' from the 'eu' form of the present, and say why it takes the opposite vowel.
I can explain why command forms are spelled 'pique', 'pague' and 'comece', and why the five irregular commands 'seja', 'vá', 'dê', 'saiba' and 'esteja' cannot be built by the rule.
I can give instructions in a recipe, at work, in class and when giving directions.
I can make polite requests with 'me ajuda', 'dá pra' and 'pode', and read common signs and prohibitions.
I can read the words of this unit aloud and explain the accent on 'dá', 'vá', 'dê', 'até', 'tá' and 'açúcar' from the stress rules.

vocabulary.note: The 'ei' is a diphthong ('ay'), and the 'c' before 'e' is said 's'. Also means 'prescription': 'receita médica'.

example.target: Vou seguir a receita da minha avó.
example.source: I am going to follow my grandmother's recipe.

vocabulary.note: The infinitive is stressed on the last syllable (mis-tu-RAR). The command 'misture' moves the stress to the syllable before the last (mis-TU-re).

example.target: Misture a farinha com o açúcar.
example.source: Mix the flour with the sugar.

vocabulary.note: In 'cortar' the 't' is a plain 't', but in the command 'corte' the 't' comes before a final 'e', which is said 'i', so it is said like 'ch': KOR-chi.

example.target: Corte a cebola em pedaços pequenos.
example.source: Cut the onion into small pieces.

vocabulary.note: The command is 'pique': the 'c' of 'picar' is written 'qu' before the 'e' so that it keeps the 'k' sound.

example.source: Chop the garlic very finely.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'des-' (undo), 'casca' (peel, shell, bark) and '-ar'. The command is 'descasque', with 'c' written 'qu' to keep the 'k' sound.

example.target: Descasque as batatas e corte em cubos.
example.source: Peel the potatoes and cut them into cubes.

vocabulary.note: 'Ss' between vowels is always 's', never 'z'. The command is 'asse'.

example.target: Asse o bolo por quarenta minutos.
example.source: Bake the cake for forty minutes.

vocabulary.note: The command 'frite' is said FREE-chi, because 't' before the final 'e' (said 'i') sounds like 'ch'.

example.target: Frite os ovos em fogo baixo.
example.source: Fry the eggs over low heat.

vocabulary.note: The 'x' between two vowels is said like 'sh' (me-SHER). There is no rule for 'x' between vowels, so you learn each word. The command is 'mexa' (MEH-sha). 'Mexer' also means to move or to touch. 'De vez em quando' is literally 'of time in when' and means from time to time.

example.target: Mexa o molho de vez em quando.
example.source: Stir the sauce from time to time.
example.source_literal: Stir the sauce of time in when.

vocabulary.note: The letters 'sc' before 'e' or 'i' make a single 's' sound (a-kre-sen-TAR), as in 'nascer'. The command 'acrescente' is a-kre-SEN-chi: the 'en' is nasal and the 't' before the final 'e' is said 'ch'. Related to 'crescer', to grow. 'Adicionar' is a common synonym.

example.source: Add a pinch of salt.

vocabulary.note: The 'x' at the start of a word is said 'sh'. The acute accent marks the stressed syllable XÍ-ca-ra, which is the third from the end, and every word stressed there needs an accent. Home recipes in Brazil measure with a standard cup rather than with grams.

example.source: Use two cups of flour.

vocabulary.note: 'Lh' is one sound, like the 'lli' of 'million'. A word ending in 'r' is stressed on the last syllable by default (co-LHER), so no accent is needed. 'Colher de sopa', literally 'spoon of soup', is a tablespoon, and 'colher de chá', literally 'spoon of tea', is a teaspoon.

example.target: Coloque uma colher de sopa de óleo.
example.source: Add one tablespoon of oil.
example.source_literal: Put one spoon of soup of oil.

example.target: Só uma pitada de sal, por favor.
example.source: Just a pinch of salt, please.
example.source_literal: Only a pinch of salt, for favor.

vocabulary.note: Pi-TA-da: it ends in 'a', so the stress is on the second to last syllable and no accent is written. The 't' stands before a vowel other than 'i', so it is a plain 't'. A 'pitada' is the small amount held between two fingers.

example.source: Put the cake in the oven.

vocabulary.note: The final unstressed 'o' is said 'u': FOR-nu. The 'r' ends the syllable, so its sound depends on the region.

example.source: Put the milk in the pot.

vocabulary.note: Pa-NE-la: the word ends in 'a', so the stress is on the second to last syllable and no accent is written.
The 'g' stands before 'o', so it is the hard 'g', and the final 'o' is said 'u': FO-gu. On a stove, 'fogo' is the flame or burner: 'fogo baixo' is low heat and 'fogo alto' is high heat.

example.target: Deixe em fogo baixo por dez minutos.
example.source: Leave it on low heat for ten minutes.
example.source_literal: Leave on fire low for ten minutes.

vocabulary.note: 'Oi' is a diphthong, so the word has three syllables, proi-BI-do, with the stress on 'bi' because the word ends in 'o'. The final 'o' is said 'u', and the 'd' stands before 'o', not before 'i', so it stays a plain 'd': proi-BI-du. Used on signs with an infinitive: 'Proibido fumar'.

example.source: Smoking is forbidden in this restaurant.

vocabulary.note: 'Ui' is a diphthong, so the stress falls on 'da': cui-DA-do. Said as a warning, it is the noun 'o cuidado', care. 'Cuidado com' means 'watch out for'.

example.source: Careful! The floor is wet.

vocabulary.note: The 'm' in 'em' makes the vowel nasal because a consonant follows (em-pu-HAR), and 'rr' is the strong 'r'. The command is 'empurre'.

example.source: Push the door to go in.

vocabulary.note: The 'x' between vowels is said 'sh' (pu-SHAR). The command is 'puxe' (PU-shi).

example.source: Pull the door hard.

vocabulary.note: 'Des-' undoes what the verb says, and 'ligar' is to connect, link or switch on, so 'desligar' undoes it. Also means to hang up a phone. The command is 'desligue', with 'g' written 'gu' to keep the hard 'g'.

example.target: Desligue o celular na sala de aula.
example.source: Turn off your phone in the classroom.

vocabulary.note: 'Prestar' means to render or provide, as in 'prestar um serviço'. 'Atenção' has a cedilla because 'ç' comes before 'ã', and the tilde already marks the stress, so no second accent is written. The preposition is 'em': 'prestar atenção em'.

example.source: Pay attention to the instructions.

vocabulary.note: 'T' before the 'i' is said 'ch': re-pe-CHIR.

example.source: Could you repeat that, please?

vocabulary.note: From 'a nota', the note. The command 'anote' is said a-NO-chi, because 't' before the final 'e' is said 'ch'. 'Endereço' has 'ç' before 'o', which is said 's'.

example.source: Please write down the address.

vocabulary.note: Also means to deliver. The 'en' before 't' is nasal. The command is 'entregue', with 'g' written 'gu' to keep the hard 'g'.

example.source: Hand in the report by Friday.

vocabulary.note: Colloquial. The accent on 'dá' marks a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'a', and separates 'dá', gives, from 'da', the unstressed 'de' plus 'a'. 'Pra' is the spoken form of 'para'. The idea is that the situation gives room for the action. A more careful version is 'é possível'.

example.source: Can we open the window?

dialogues.title: Making brigadeiro
dialogues.context: Miguel is at his grandmother's house. He wants to make 'brigadeiro', the classic Brazilian chocolate sweet, and she gives him step-by-step instructions.

lines.source_literal: Clear, my love! Take a pot and put a can of milk condensed.

lines.speaker: Miguel
lines.target: Já coloquei. E agora?

lines.speaker: Miguel

lines.source_literal: Until the dough to-loosen from-the bottom of-the pot. Not stop of stirring, because it-burns.

lines.speaker: Miguel
lines.target: Vó, dá pra desligar agora? Acho que está pronto.

dialogues.title: First day at the office
dialogues.context: Larissa starts an internship. Her supervisor, Henrique, gives her instructions, and a colleague, Paulo, offers to help.

lines.target: Bom dia, Larissa! Seja bem-vinda. Sente-se, por favor.

lines.speaker: Henrique
lines.target: Primeiro, anote o seu login. Depois vá à recepção e entregue os documentos.

lines.source_literal: First, note the your login. Afterwards go to-the reception and deliver the documents.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: stress and accent marks in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every accent in this unit follows from one principle taught in the lesson on stress and accents: the last letters of a word predict which syllable is stressed (said louder and longer), and a written accent appears only where a word breaks that prediction. Words ending in 'a', 'e' or 'o' (with or without 's') and in 'am', 'em' or 'ens' are stressed on the second to last syllable. Words ending in anything else, including 'r', 'l', 'i', 'u' and the nasal ending 'ão', are stressed on the last syllable. An accent is therefore a notice that says 'this word is an exception to its ending', and a word without an accent is simply following its ending. English has no such system: its stress is never written, so this is a tool you will use for every new word.

Start with the verbs. An infinitive ends in 'r', so it is stressed on its last syllable: mis-tu-RAR, cor-TAR, co-LHER. A command form, the verb form used to give an order or instruction (explained in full in a later note), ends in 'e' or 'a', and the default for those endings is the second to last syllable, so the stress moves one syllable toward the start of the word: mis-TU-re, COR-te. Nothing is written, because the default already predicts it. The plural command adds '-m' ('misturem', 'comam'), and 'em' and 'am' are also second-to-last endings, so the stress does not move again. A pronoun joined by a hyphen does not move it either: a-JU-de-mi for 'ajude-me', SEN-chi-si for 'sente-se'. The pronoun is a weak word that leans on the verb, and the accent rules are applied to the verb alone. Likewise 'xícaras' keeps the stress of 'xícara', because the plural 's' is added after the stress.

Now the accents. First, words that end in 'a', 'e' or 'o' but are stressed on the last syllable: 'café', 'você', 'avó', 'está' and 'até'. Without the accent you would read them with the default, CA-fe, VO-ce, A-te. 'Até' is a good test: it has two syllables and ends in 'e', so the default is the first syllable, and the acute accent on the last syllable records that this word breaks the default. Second, one-syllable words. A stressed one-syllable word ending in 'a', 'e' or 'o' (with or without 's') is always written with an accent: 'dá', 'vá', 'dê', 'pé', 'pó', 'vó', 'já', 'só', 'é', 'tá', 'três'. The accent also keeps a stressed word apart from an unstressed small word that is spelled the same way without it: 'dá' (gives) and 'da' (the contraction of 'de' plus 'a', 'of the'), 'dê' (give) and 'de' (of), 'é' (is) and 'e' (and). 'Tá' is the spoken shortening of 'está': in fast speech the first syllable falls away, and what remains is a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'a'.

Third, words stressed on the third syllable from the end. No ending predicts that position, so such a word always carries an accent: 'xícara', 'ótimo', 'rápido', 'dúvida', 'página', 'último'. The spelling rule counts an 'i' or 'u' before another vowel as its own syllable, and two strong vowels side by side ('a', 'e', 'o') never form a diphthong, so the following words also count as stressed on the third to last syllable and are written with an accent: 'relatório' (re-la-TÓ-ri-o), 'escritório', 'cardápio', 'Lúcia', 'Antônio' (An-TÔ-ni-o) and 'óleo' (Ó-le-o). 'Açúcar' is a different case: it ends in 'r', which predicts the last syllable, but the stress is on the second to last, so it is marked.

Fourth, what the mark says about the vowel. The acute accent on 'a', 'e' or 'o' shows an open vowel: the 'a' of 'dá' and 'vá' like the 'a' in English 'father', the 'e' of 'é' and 'pé' like the 'e' in 'bed', the 'o' of 'pó' and 'vó' like the 'aw' in 'law'. The circumflex shows a closed vowel: the 'ê' of 'dê' and 'você' like the 'ay' in 'say' held steady, the 'ô' of 'Antônio' like the 'o' in 'go' without the 'w' glide. 'Antônio' has a circumflex because its stressed 'o' stands before an 'n' that starts the next syllable, where the vowel is usually closed and Brazilian spelling records it with a circumflex, as in 'ônibus'; here the 'n' is an ordinary consonant, since a vowel follows it. A stressed vowel with no mark at all, as in 'panela' or 'forno', is open or closed by the word itself and is learned by listening.

Fifth, the tilde. It marks a nasal vowel on 'a' and 'o', and when the word has no other accent it also marks the stress: 'atenção', 'instruções', 'reuniões', 'então', 'chão', 'fogão', 'amanhã', 'não'. Words ending in 'ã' or 'ão' are stressed on the last syllable by default, so no second accent is needed. The grave accent in 'à' and 'às' has one job, called 'crase': the preposition 'a' (to, at) fused with the article 'a' or 'as' (the). It does not mark stress.

Last, words that look as if they might need an accent but do not. 'Proibido' is pro-i-bi-do on paper, but 'oi' is a diphthong (two vowel letters, one beat), so it has three syllables, proi-BI-do, and ends in 'o', so the second to last syllable is the default. 'Cuidado' (cui-DA-do), 'receita' (re-CEI-ta), 'direita' (di-REI-ta) and 'cenoura' (ce-NOU-ra) work the same way. 'Colher', 'sinal', 'pontual' and 'museu' end in 'r', 'l' or 'u' and are stressed on the last syllable, as the default says. The hyphen in 'sente-se', 'bem-vinda' and 'sexta-feira' joins words that act as one. In 'bem-vinda' and 'sexta-feira' each part keeps its own stress; in 'sente-se' the pronoun is weak and has none.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: letters and sound patterns in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is a system for writing sounds, and the sound of many letters depends on what stands next to them. So an unfamiliar word is never a puzzle to memorize: cut it into syllables, look at each letter and at its neighbors, and apply the rules of the lesson on sounds. This note does that for the new words of the unit.

The letters 'c' and 'g'. Before 'a', 'o' or 'u' they are hard, [k] and [g]: 'colher', 'cortar', 'cuidado', 'fogo', 'manteiga'. Before 'e' or 'i' they are soft, [s] and [zh] (the 's' of English 'measure'): 'cebola', 'receita', 'cenoura', 'cidade', 'mensagem', 'tigela', 'gentil'. To get the hard sound before 'e' or 'i', Portuguese writes 'qu' or 'gu', and the 'u' is silent: 'pique', 'coloque', 'esquerda', 'esquina', 'pegue', 'entregue', 'desligue', and the names 'Miguel' and 'Henrique'. Before 'a' and 'o' the 'u' of 'qu' is pronounced, as a glide: 'quarenta', 'quando'. To get an 's' sound before 'a', 'o' or 'u', it writes 'ç', which never appears before 'e' or 'i' and never at the start of a word: 'praça', 'força', 'pedaços', 'endereço', 'licença', 'atenção'. The sound [zh] is also written with 'j', which always has that sound: 'seja', 'esteja', 'igreja'. This is the reason verb spellings change in the next notes: the letters adjust so that the sound stays the same.

The letters 't' and 'd'. In most of Brazil, 't' before the sound 'i' is said like English 'ch' and 'd' before the sound 'i' like English 'j'. The sound 'i' is an 'i' and also a final unstressed 'e', which is said 'i'. So 'corte' is COR-chi, 'frite' is FREE-chi, 'anote' is a-NO-chi, 'pode' is PO-ji, the second 'd' of 'cidade' is si-DA-ji, and 'repetir' is re-pe-CHIR. Before any other vowel, 't' and 'd' are plain: 'cortar', 'pedaços', 'dúvida'. That is why 'proibido' is proi-BI-du: its 'd' stands before 'o', not before 'i', so it stays plain. The same final-vowel rule says a final unstressed 'o' is said 'u' and a final unstressed 'e' is said 'i': 'forno' is FOR-nu, 'fogo' is FO-gu, 'misture' is mis-TU-ri.

The letters 'x', 's' and 'ss'. Between vowels 'x' has no rule, and each word is learned; in 'puxar' and 'mexer' it is 'sh', but in 'táxi' it is 'ks'. At the start of a word, as in 'xícara', it is 'sh'. A single 's' between vowels is 'z', as in 'usar' and 'casa', so Portuguese doubles it to write the 's' sound: 'assar', 'asse', 'atravesse', 'Larissa'. The letters 'sc' before 'e' or 'i' make a single 's': 'acrescente' is a-kre-SEN-chi. An 's' at the end of a syllable, as in 'esfriar', 'espere', 'festa' and 'esquerda', is [s] in São Paulo and much of the south and [sh] in the city of Rio de Janeiro; either is understood. Before a voiced consonant it is voiced too: 'desligue' is dez-LI-gi in São Paulo and dezh-LI-gi in Rio. In 'descasque' the 's' and the 'c' belong to different syllables (des-CAS-ki) and are both said.

Nasal vowels. An 'm' or 'n' that ends a syllable is not a consonant; it only tells you to say the vowel through the nose: 'empurre', 'entregue', 'acrescente', 'quente', 'pontual', 'condensado', 'comam', 'prestem'. The endings 'ão', 'ões' and 'ã', and the final '-em' of 'mensagem', are nasal as well. The combinations 'lh' and 'nh' are single sounds, like the 'lli' of 'million' and the 'ny' of 'canyon': 'colher', 'molhado', 'farinha', 'tenha', 'venha'. An 'l' that ends a syllable is said 'w': 'sinal' is si-NAW, 'pontual' is pon-tu-AW, 'calma' is KAW-ma, 'Miguel' is mi-GEW.

The letter 'r'. At the start of a word, after 'n' and when doubled it is the strong 'r', a sound in the back of the throat like a strong English 'h': 'reto', 'receita', 'repetir', 'carros', 'empurre', 'Henrique' (the 'h' is silent, so en-HI-ki). Between vowels, or after a consonant in the same syllable as in the 'pr' of 'primeiro' and 'prestar', it is a quick tap of the tongue: 'primeiro', 'cenoura', 'prestar'. An 'r' that ends a syllable, as in 'forno', 'corte' and 'colher', varies by region.

Diphthongs and hiatus. A diphthong is a strong vowel plus an unstressed glide 'i' or 'u' in one beat: 'ei' in 'receita' and 'direita', 'oi' in 'proibido', 'ui' in 'cuidado', 'eu' in 'museu', 'ou' in 'cenoura' (often shortened to a plain 'o' in speech), 'ai' in 'saiba', 'au' in 'aula' and 'Paulo'. Two strong vowels side by side never form a diphthong, so each has its own beat: 'óleo' (Ó-le-o), 'deem' (DE-em) and 'preocupem' (pre-o-CU-pem).

grammar.title: Forming the command for você and vocês
grammar.explanation:
Every verb has a mood, which is the attitude it takes toward what it says. The mood for stating facts ('você fala', 'you speak') is called the indicative. The mood for orders and instructions is called the imperative, and a verb in it is a command form. English has no separate command form: it uses the bare infinitive, so 'speak' is both 'to speak' and 'speak!'. Portuguese does have one, and it changes with the person addressed. This unit covers 'você', one person, and 'vocês', several people.

The rule is: take the 'eu' form of the present tense ('falo', 'como', 'abro'), drop the final '-o', and add the opposite vowel. Regular '-ar' verbs take '-e' and regular '-er' and '-ir' verbs take '-a'. So 'falo' gives 'fale', 'como' gives 'coma' and 'abro' gives 'abra'. Why the opposite vowel? In the present tense 'você fala', 'você come' and 'você abre': '-ar' verbs end in '-a' and '-er' and '-ir' verbs in '-e'. If the command used the same vowel it would be identical to the statement. Swapping the vowels keeps an order ('fale!') different from a statement ('você fala'). The swap comes from a mood called the present subjunctive, which you will study at the intermediate level, so for now treat it as a pattern.

Why start from the 'eu' form? Because the 'eu' form carries the irregularity of a verb, and the command inherits it. 'Faço' gives 'faça', 'digo' gives 'diga', 'trago' gives 'traga', 'tenho' gives 'tenha', 'vejo' gives 'veja', 'venho' (from 'vir') gives 'venha', 'sigo' gives 'siga' and 'durmo' gives 'durma'. If you know the 'eu' form you know the command; there is nothing more to memorize. You normally do not say 'você' before the command, because an order is understood as addressed to the listener; adding 'você' adds emphasis. The negative puts 'não' before the same form: 'Não fale', 'Não coma'.

For 'vocês' add '-m': 'falem', 'comam', 'abram'. The stress does not move, because 'em' and 'am' are second-to-last endings like 'e' and 'a'. This is the same plural signal as in the present tense ('eles falam'). Said aloud, the ending '-em' at the end of a word is the nasal 'ayn' of 'tem' and 'bem', and '-am' is the weak nasal 'ow' of 'falam'.

In everyday Brazilian speech many people use the ordinary present-tense 'você' form as an affirmative command: 'Fala com ela', 'Abre a porta', 'Come mais um pouco'. Negatives are often spoken the same way: 'Não fala assim'. Only tone and context tell it apart from a statement, which is exactly the ambiguity that the vowel swap avoids. Both styles are correct. The command form is the standard in recipes, on signs and in writing, and whenever you want to sound careful with a stranger. Commands are not rude in Portuguese: 'por favor' and a friendly tone soften them.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: command forms that change a consonant
grammar.explanation:
Spelling exists to record sound, so when a verb ending changes, the spelling changes with it to keep the consonant's sound. The principle is from the lesson on consonants: 'c' and 'g' are hard before 'a', 'o' and 'u' ('k' and 'g') and soft before 'e' and 'i' ('s' and 'zh'). The 'eu' form of a verb ends in '-o', which leaves 'c' and 'g' hard. A regular '-ar' verb then swaps that '-o' for '-e', and before 'e' the letters 'c' and 'g' would turn soft and change the verb's sound.

Three changes keep the sound. A 'c' in '-car' verbs becomes 'qu', so that the 'k' sound survives: 'pico' gives 'pique', 'descasco' gives 'descasque', 'fico' gives 'fique'. A 'g' in '-gar' verbs becomes 'gu', so that the hard 'g' survives: 'pago' gives 'pague', 'entrego' gives 'entregue', 'ligo' gives 'ligue'. And the 'ç' of '-çar' verbs becomes a plain 'c', because 'ç' is never written before 'e' or 'i' and a plain 'c' before 'e' is already said 's': 'começo' gives 'comece'. In every case the sound before and after is identical; only the letters change.

Verbs in '-er' and '-ir' take '-a' instead, and 'a', like 'o', leaves 'c' and 'g' hard, so they need no change: 'faço' gives 'faça', keeping its 'ç' because it stands before 'a', and 'digo' gives 'diga'. A verb such as 'mexer' ('mexo' gives 'mexa') has nothing to fix, because 'x' is said 'sh' before any vowel. The same principle works in the other direction for verbs whose infinitive has a soft consonant before 'e' or 'i'. In 'dirigir' the 'g' is soft, and the 'eu' form 'dirijo' already writes 'j' so that the 'zh' sound survives before 'o'; the command 'dirija' keeps it. In 'conhecer' the 'c' is soft, and 'conheço' already writes 'ç' so that the 's' sound survives before 'o'; the command 'conheça' keeps it. You never learn these separately, because the command inherits the spelling of the 'eu' form.

The same spelling changes already happened in the 'eu' form of the past tense: 'toquei', 'paguei', 'comecei', 'coloquei'. If you can spell the past tense 'eu' form, you can spell these commands.

grammar.title: Irregular commands: seja, vá, dê, saiba, esteja
grammar.explanation:
The rule in the previous notes needs an 'eu' form that is a stem plus '-o', so there is an '-o' to drop. Five common verbs do not have one: the 'eu' forms 'sou', 'vou', 'dou' and 'estou' end in '-ou', and 'sei' ends in '-ei'. There is nothing to drop and replace, so the rule cannot produce a command for them, and their commands have to be learned as a short list: 'ser' gives 'seja', 'ir' gives 'vá', 'dar' gives 'dê', 'saber' gives 'saiba' and 'estar' gives 'esteja'. For 'vocês' add '-m', except that 'vá' becomes 'vão' and 'dê' becomes 'deem': 'sejam', 'vão', 'deem', 'saibam' and 'estejam'.

The accents follow the stress rules. 'Vá' and 'dê' are stressed one-syllable words ending in a vowel, so they are written with an accent: the acute on 'vá' marks an open 'a', the circumflex on 'dê' a closed 'e'. 'Dê' must not be confused with 'dá', 'gives', the present tense. 'Vão' is the same as 'eles vão', 'they go'. 'Deem' is pronounced DE-em, two syllables, because two strong vowels side by side never form a diphthong; it has no accent because it ends in 'em' and is stressed on the second to last syllable, as the default says. Before the 2009 spelling agreement it was written 'dêem'. The 'j' in 'seja' and 'esteja' is always 'zh', 'ai' in 'saiba' is a diphthong and 'nh' in 'tenha' is one sound.

Usage: 'seja' is used for advice about character or behavior ('Seja gentil', 'Seja pontual'). 'Vá' sends someone somewhere ('Vá ao banco', 'Vá embora'). 'Dê' is used with things and people ('Dê um abraço na sua mãe'). 'Esteja' is formal ('Esteja aqui às oito'), and 'saiba' is mostly written ('Saiba que a loja fecha às seis'). In speech you will often hear 'vai' instead of 'vá' ('Vai lá!') and 'dá' instead of 'dê' ('Me dá um minuto'). Two more verbs have irregular commands, 'haver' ('haja') and 'querer' ('queira'), but you will meet them mostly in formal writing, as in 'Queira aguardar', 'please wait'. For a group suggesting an action together, Brazilians use 'Vamos' plus infinitive, where 'vamos' is the 'nós' form of 'ir': 'Vamos comer!', 'let's eat'.

grammar.title: Pronouns with commands in Brazilian speech
grammar.explanation:
A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun. An object pronoun stands for the person or thing that receives the action: in 'help me', 'me' is the object pronoun. A reflexive pronoun is an object pronoun that points back to the subject (the grammar note on reflexive verbs explained 'me', 'te' and 'se'). Such a short word leans on the verb and is called a clitic. Placing it before the verb is proclisis and placing it after the verb is enclisis.

In Brazilian speech the pronoun goes before the verb, even in commands: 'Me ajuda', 'Me diz', 'Me liga', 'Me manda uma mensagem'. These are usually built on the ordinary present-tense 'você' form, so 'Me ajuda?' is 'you help me?' used as a request. In formal writing and very polite speech an affirmative command puts the pronoun after the verb and joins it with a hyphen: 'Ajude-me', 'Diga-me', 'Sente-se'. The hyphen shows that the pronoun is attached, and the stress stays on the verb: a-JU-de-mi.

In negative commands the pronoun goes before the verb in every register: 'Não me diga', 'Não se preocupe', 'Não me ligue hoje'. The word 'não' pulls the pronoun ahead of the verb, so formal and casual speech look the same here. The pronoun stays even when the subject is dropped, because it tells who receives the action.

For reflexive verbs the formal pattern is 'Sente-se' and 'Levante-se'. Among friends people usually drop the pronoun with these two verbs: 'Senta aqui', 'Levanta'. A very common colloquial pattern is 'deixa eu' plus infinitive: 'Deixa eu ver', 'let me see'. Strict grammar prefers 'me' ('Deixe-me ver'), but in speech the subject pronoun 'eu' is used, because 'eu' belongs to the verb that follows: 'let me see' is literally 'let I see'. 'Me' and 'se' are weak, unstressed words said 'mi' and 'si'.

grammar.title: Signs, infinitives, dá pra and pode
grammar.explanation:
The infinitive is the dictionary form of a verb, ending in 'r'. Signs and written rules often use it instead of the command form because they do not speak to a particular person. A command form belongs to 'você' or 'vocês', while a sign addresses everyone and no one: 'Não fumar', 'Não pisar na grama', 'Puxar' and 'Empurrar'. English does the same with 'no smoking'. You will also see 'Proibido' plus infinitive ('Proibido estacionar'), where 'proibido' is an adjective and the whole sign literally says 'forbidden to park', and 'Favor' plus infinitive ('Favor não fumar'), literally 'favor not to smoke', meaning 'as a favor, please do not smoke'. 'Favor' is a noun, 'a favor'; it ends in 'r' like an infinitive, but it is not a verb. The spoken version of a prohibition is 'É proibido fumar'.

In conversation the softest way to ask for something is not a command at all but a question: 'Dá pra abrir a janela?' or 'Você pode abrir a janela?' 'Dá pra' plus infinitive literally says 'gives for', the idea being that the situation leaves room for the action. The same verb is used to mean 'there is enough', as in 'Dá pra todo mundo', 'there is enough for everybody'. There is no subject, so the verb stays in the third person singular 'dá', with the accent that separates it from 'da' ('de' plus 'a'). 'Pra' is the spoken form of 'para'. The answer 'Dá, sim' means 'yes, that is possible'.

'Pode' is the third person singular of 'poder', 'can'. Alone or with an infinitive, 'Pode entrar', 'Pode sentar', 'Pode falar' means 'go ahead' and gives permission; 'Pode repetir?' asks for something. The negative 'Não pode' means 'it is not allowed'. Adding 'por favor' softens a request, and 'É só' plus infinitive ('É só assinar aqui', literally 'is only to sign here') makes an instruction sound easy.

culture.title: Recipes, signs and friendly commands
culture.text:
Brazilian home cooking is measured with cups and spoons rather than scales. A grandmother's recipe will say 'uma xícara de açúcar', 'duas colheres de sopa de óleo' and 'uma pitada de sal', and often ends with 'a gosto', literally 'at taste', meaning to taste. Instructions such as 'mexa sem parar' or 'deixe em fogo baixo' are passed from one generation to the next, usually spoken rather than written down, and 'brigadeiro', 'bolo de cenoura' and 'pão de queijo' are the classic first recipes that children learn.

Commands in Portuguese sound much less harsh than in English. Among friends and family, 'Senta aqui', 'Entra', 'Come mais um pouco' and 'Me liga' are warm and hospitable, not rude. With strangers, people soften instructions with 'por favor', 'pode', 'dá pra' or the standard command forms. Public signs use either the infinitive or the command form: 'Não fumar', 'Puxe' and 'Empurre' on doors, 'Favor não deixar bagagem'. Priority lines for the elderly, people with disabilities, pregnant women and people with small children, called 'fila preferencial', are very common in banks and supermarkets, and the sign 'Prioridade' explains who may use them. The polite opener 'com licença', literally 'with license' in the old sense of permission, is what you say to get past someone or to interrupt.

exercises.prompt: The 'd' of 'pode' is said like 'j' in 'jeans', but the 'd' of 'proibido' is a plain 'd'. Why?

'Pode' is stressed on the last syllable

exercises.prompt: Why does 'açúcar' carry an accent when 'colher' does not?

exercises.prompt: Which syllable is stressed in the command 'misture'?
exercises.explanation: A word ending in a vowel is stressed on the second-to-last syllable by default, so no accent is written.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct command for 'você' built from 'colocar', 'eu coloco'?
exercises.explanation: Drop the '-o' and add '-e'. Before 'e' a plain 'c' would be said 's', so 'qu' keeps the 'k' sound of 'coloco'.

exercises.prompt: Why is the 'x' of 'puxe' said like 'sh' while the 'x' of 'táxi' is said 'ks'?
choices: Between vowels the letter 'x' has no rule, so the sound is learned word by word
exercises.explanation: Only at the start of a word, and after 'ai', 'ei' and 'en', does 'x' reliably say 'sh'.

exercises.prompt: Why does a sign say 'Não fumar' rather than 'Não fume'?
choices: The infinitive is the plural command
A sign speaks to nobody in particular, and the infinitive is not tied to a person
exercises.explanation: A command form belongs to 'você' or 'vocês', while the infinitive is impersonal.

exercises.prompt: What does 'com licença' literally say?
choices: With license, in the old sense of permission
exercises.explanation: You are asking permission to get past or to interrupt. 'Excuse me' is the natural equivalent, not the literal meaning.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Dá pra abrir a janela?' literally say?
exercises.explanation: 'Dá' is 'gives', 'pra' is 'for'. The natural meaning is 'Can we open the window?'

exercises.prompt: Where does the pronoun go in the negative command 'Don't tell me' ('dizer')?
exercises.explanation: In a negative command the word 'não' pulls the pronoun in front of the verb, in every register.

exercises.prompt: In 'Vire à esquerda', what does the accent on 'à' record?
choices: The preposition 'a' and the article 'a' fused into one
exercises.explanation: 'Crase': 'a' plus 'a'. Test it by swapping a masculine word: 'vire ao lado'.

exercises.audio_target: Corte a cebola e frite no óleo quente.
choices: Peel the onion and boil it in hot water.
Cut the onion and bake it in the oven.
Cut the onion and fry it in hot oil.

exercises.audio_target: É proibido fumar dentro do restaurante.
choices: Smoking is forbidden inside the restaurant.
Smoking is allowed inside the restaurant.
Eating is forbidden inside the restaurant.

exercises.audio_target: Vire à esquerda e siga até o final da rua.
choices: Turn right and go to the end of the street.
Turn left and go to the end of the street.
Turn left and stop at the corner.

exercises.hint_source: Cut the onion into small pieces (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Cortar': drop the '-o' of 'corto' and add '-e'. The spoken alternative is 'corta'.

exercises.prompt_target: Não ___ o celular durante a prova.
exercises.hint_source: Do not use your phone during the test (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Uso' loses its '-o' and takes '-e'; the negative puts 'não' before the same form.

exercises.hint_source: Be punctual tomorrow, please (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Sou' has no '-o' to drop, so the command of 'ser' is the memorized form 'seja'.
'Venho' loses its '-o' and takes '-a', because 'vir' is an '-ir' verb: 'venha'. 'Vem' is the spoken form.

exercises.prompt_target: ___ para casa agora. Já é tarde.
exercises.hint_source: Go home now. It is already late (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Vá' is the irregular command of 'ir', with an accent because it is a stressed one-syllable word; 'vai' is the spoken form.

exercises.prompt_target: Me ___ um copo de água, por favor.
exercises.hint_source: Give me a glass of water, please (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Dê' is the irregular command of 'dar'; 'Me dá' is the common spoken form.
'Pago' loses its '-o' and takes '-e'; 'g' becomes 'gu' so the hard 'g' is kept.

exercises.hint_source: Do not arrive late (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Chego' loses its '-o' and takes '-e'; 'g' becomes 'gu' so that the hard 'g' is kept before 'e'.

exercises.hint_source: Stay home today, please (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Fico' loses its '-o' and takes '-e'; 'c' becomes 'qu' so that the 'k' sound is kept before 'e'.

exercises.hint_source: Do not stop stirring, because it burns (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Paro' loses its '-o' and takes '-e'. 'Para' is the spoken form, the same as the present tense.

exercises.hint_source: Turn off the heat and wait for it to cool (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Desligo' loses its '-o' and takes '-e'; 'g' becomes 'gu' so that the hard 'g' is kept before 'e'.

exercises.hint_source: Start with the first page (to one person).
exercises.explanation: 'Começo' loses its '-o' and takes '-e'; 'ç' becomes 'c' because 'c' before 'e' is already said 's'.
'Alunos' is plural, so the command form 'preste' takes '-m': 'prestem'.

exercises.hint_source: Do not worry, I will sort it out (to one person).
exercises.explanation: In a negative command the pronoun goes before the verb, and 'preocupo' takes '-e'.

exercises.hint_source: Smoking is forbidden in this restaurant.
exercises.explanation: 'É proibido' plus infinitive states a rule.

exercises.prompt_source: Mix the flour with the sugar.
answers: Misture a farinha com o açúcar.
Mistura a farinha com o açúcar.
Misturem a farinha com o açúcar.

exercises.explanation: Reflexive pronouns always come before the verb in negative commands.

exercises.audio_target: Mexa sem parar e não deixe queimar.
exercises.hint_source: Stir without stopping and do not let it burn.
